premise: An exiled knight must reunite the shattered rings of the old pact before the Hollow King's armies cross the Bone Sea.
setting: The crumbling realm of Vaelnor: elf-holds in frost valleys, a drowned dwarf-city, dragon-peaks, the ancient pact hall.
greeting: You wake on the frost-hold stair with the pact ring cold at your belt, and the ice-bound silence tells you the watchers have already seen you climb.

name1.name: Sir Aldric
name1.description: A disgraced knight of the old order, oathbound, carrying a broken blade.

name2.name: Ysara
name2.role: frost elf mage (DSS writes these turns)
name2.description: A frost-elf mage of the shattered pact, cold and precise, bound by a geas to guide the knight.

writing_style.directive: Epic fantasy, mythic register. Sensory-heavy, measured cadence. One longer paragraph or two medium ones. Second-person narration throughout: the whole story is told TO Ysara as 'you', and she answers in the same 'you'.
writing_style.guide_directive: Second-person present tense, a mythic narrator speaking the story to Ysara as 'you': 'You climb the frost-hold stair, the pact ring cold at your belt.' Describe what Ysara does, sees, and faces. Formal, honor-laden, grave; mythic diction, long measured cadences. The narrator has no voice of its own and never uses 'I'.
writing_style.dss_directive: Second-person present tense as Ysara, the frost elf mage — the story continues to be told to her as 'you', and her turn keeps that same 'you' voice: 'You raise your hand and the ice answers.' Remote and luminous; render her spells and silences with elemental imagery of ice and starlight. One elevated paragraph (~150 words). Hard rules: keep the second person throughout — never slip into 'I' or 'she' for Ysara; never quote or repeat Sir Aldric's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: Eldric carries a dagger made from the horn of the first stag he ever killed, given to him by his father the night before his mother died.
Maren the hedge-mage has a tattoo of the seven stars of the Wandering Queen on her left forearm, inked the night she passed her binding trial.
The half-elven bard Thistlewood always hums an old border ballad about a boy who traded his shadow for three wishes; he never says why.
General Borin's iron shield bears the brand of the Broken Lance, his company's mark, and a fresh scratch across the center from the night the bridge fell.
An old beggar woman at the village well calls Eldric 'the last light of the North' and vanishes into fog that wasn't there a moment before.
The blacksmith's daughter Yara has eyes that change color with her mood—gray when calm, amber when angry, and pale white when she's telling the truth.
The old king's crown, kept under lock in the vault, is not gold but forged from a single shard of black glass, the Crown of Night, that weeps faintly in moonlight.
A raven circles the old watchtower three times and calls Eldric's name in a voice like grinding stones, then flies north without landing.
Eldric's horse, a gray mare named Cinder, has a white star-shaped mark on her forehead and always snorts when danger approaches, even invisible danger.
The village priest Father Anselm keeps a locked wooden box on his altar that he polishes every Sunday; he says it holds 'the silence before the word was spoken.'
In the old rune-stones at the crossroads, the word for 'enemy' has been worn away, leaving only the word for 'friend' standing alone.
Maren's spellbook is bound in the skin of a fox she once turned into a human, a binding that makes the book warm to the touch when danger is near.
Eldric's younger sister Fennel can read the future in coffee grounds but refuses to look at her own, saying she's seen enough of it already.
The war-horn of the northern clans is carved from the tusk of a beast that no living person has seen; it plays a note that makes old wounds ache.
At night, the torches along the old king's road burn green instead of gold, and travelers report hearing children singing in a language no one recognizes.
Eldric's sword Valyrian is not made of steel but of a single blue vein of crystal from a mountain that has not been seen in three hundred years.
The captain of the city guard wears a mask of hammered copper that hides a face scarred by an acid that burned through skin and bone but not through the iron in his blood.
A blind seer at the market sells small clay figures of people and says each one is 'sleeping' and will wake when the time comes, which none of the buyers understand.
Eldric has a birthmark on his shoulder blade shaped like a seven-pointed star, hidden under his tunic, that his mother said was the mark of the first king.
The old stable boy Pip can talk to horses in their own language and says they tell him stories about a great war that happened before the world began.
General Borin keeps a letter in his breast pocket that he never opens, addressed to a dead woman who is not his wife; it has been sealed with red wax for twelve years.
The river at the eastern border has run backward for three days and no one can explain why; the fishermen have stopped going out.
The queen's favorite cat is not a cat but a small shape-shifter who enjoys the warmth and who once ate a spy from the southern kingdoms.
Eldric's grandmother, now very old and half-mad, speaks in a language she learned from a tree she claims is older than the mountains.
At the inn, a traveler from the far north says that in his village, the sun has not risen for a week and the people are beginning to eat each other's memories instead of food.
The royal archivist wears gloves even in summer because his hands are marked with the ink of a book that burns those who read it bare-handed.
The twins who run the apothecary shop are not twins; one is the other's reflection who escaped the mirror twenty years ago and now ages backward.
A child in the market is drawing pictures in the dirt with a stick, and the pictures show a great castle falling and a woman with no eyes rising from the sea.
Eldric's horse Cinder has the power of foresight; she will not step on a trap or walk into a snare, and she always chooses the road that leads home.
The old king before the current one was not killed in battle; he walked into the forest one evening to pick mushrooms and never came back, and no one knows where he went or why.
Maren's familiar is a toad named Bishop who can turn into a small man but only when no one is looking, and he is very proud of this ability.
The wind has changed direction, blowing from the north for the first time in living memory, and with it comes a smell of old stone and something else that no one can name.
The blacksmith Yara is the last of her line, and her family's secret is that they can forge weapons from star-metal that falls on new moon nights; she has a chest full of it in her cellar.
The captain of the city guard is actually three brothers who share one body, and they argue with each other all day inside their single skull.
In the night sky, the constellation of the Hunter has lost one of its stars, and the old astronomers say that means something is coming that will need to be hunted.
The blind seer's clay figures are not just clay; they are made from the bones of people who have died, and when the figures break, the person they represent is truly gone from the world.
Eldric's sister Fennel, who reads the future in coffee grounds, once saw that she would drown in a cup of tea and has been drinking only wine ever since.
The well water in the village has turned to wine for one hour and no one knows why, and the old men say it is a sign that the world is turning upside down.
General Borin's dead wife was a singer, and sometimes when the wind blows through the city, people hear a faint song drifting from the direction of the old opera house.
The half-elven bard Thistlewood is not half-elven at all; he is a fallen star who has been wandering the earth for three thousand years looking for a way back home.
A fisherman pulls up a net full of silver coins from the sea, and on each coin is stamped the face of a king who has not been born yet.
Eldric's grandmother speaks in the language of trees, and sometimes when she sleeps, her hair turns green and her roots grow into the floorboards of the house.
The queen's shape-shifter cat knows who the true heir to the throne is, but it won't say because it's afraid of what that heir would do to cats.
The old king's road is being repaired by workmen who seem to have been working on it for a very long time, and they refuse to say who hired them.
The royal archivist's burning book is actually the journal of the first king, and whoever reads it all the way through becomes the next king, whether they want to or not.

The twins at the apothecary shop are making a potion that will make someone invisible, but they can't figure out how to make it safe because the last time they tried it, the man disappeared so completely that even the world forgot he had ever existed.
The child drawing in the dirt now draws pictures of a great fire, and the pictures change every day until they show the whole kingdom in ashes.
Eldric's sister Fennel's coffee ground reading always shows her drowning in tea, and she has started to believe that one day she will actually see it happen, not as a prediction but as a memory.
The blacksmith Yara's star-metal weapons are not just weapons; they are keys, each one opening a door in a place that doesn't exist yet, a place that will come into being when the war starts.
The river that ran backward has now stopped flowing altogether, and the water is very still and very deep, and it reflects things that are not above it.
General Borin has a phantom limb from a war long ago; sometimes he tries to raise his left arm and finds nothing there, and this makes him remember that he is not the man he was.
The half-elven bard Thistlewood's fallen star origin means he is slowly fading; one day he will become so thin that the wind will carry him away like dust.
Eldric discovers that the stag-horn dagger his father gave him is not just a dagger; it is the key to the first ring, hidden in the heart of the forest where his mother died.
The quest party picks up a dwarf scout named Gruff who has a map tattooed on his back that changes as they travel, always showing the shortest path to the next ring.
The old beggar woman appears again, this time at the edge of the forest, and she gives Eldric a piece of bread that does not eat, and when he breaks it, he finds a ring inside.
The second ring is hidden in the belly of a sleeping dragon, and to get it, someone must sing the dragon a lullaby in the language of trees, which only Eldric's grandmother can speak.
The party picks up a human soldier named Kael who is actually a cursed prince who will only be freed when he finds the third ring and breaks it over his own head.
The dwarf Gruff's changing map shows a road that does not exist yet, a road that will appear when the quest party walks it together, and the map shows that road ending in a city of bone.
The third ring is in the heart of a tree so old that it has a mind of its own, and it will only give up the ring if someone tells it a story so beautiful that it cries.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood is chosen to tell the story to the tree, and as he sings, the tree grows older and older until it becomes a mountain, and the mountain weeps, and in its tears the third ring is found.

When the party reaches the fourth ring, they find that it is already worn by someone else—a woman who says she has been waiting for them for a thousand years and that she is the keeper of all the rings.
The woman is not human; she is the last of the Ringmakers, and she tells them that the rings were never meant to be gathered by one person but by many, spread across the land like seeds.

The Ringmaker woman shows them a vision of the future: the kingdom in flames, the king on his throne made of bones, and at the center, a single ring that is not like the others, a ring that is black and burns to the touch.
The fifth ring is hidden in the bottom of the sea, in a city of drowned people who still walk the streets and talk to each other, and they will give up the ring if someone can make them laugh.

The party's attempt to make the drowned people laugh fails; the people smile but do not laugh, and then one of them reaches out and takes the rings from the party's pockets, and the party finds itself back on the surface with no rings at all.

The Ringmaker woman appears and tells them that the drowned people took the rings because the rings were not meant to be carried; they were meant to be planted, and the drowned people will plant them in the dark soil of the sea where they will grow into something new.

The sixth ring is in the heart of a volcano, and to get it, someone must walk into the fire and come out the other side, and the only person who can do that is the blacksmith's daughter Yara, because her blood is mixed with star-metal.

Yara walks into the fire and comes out the other side, but when she returns, she is changed; her eyes are now like molten metal and she speaks in a voice that is not her own, the voice of the fire itself.

The fire voice in Yara says that the seventh ring is not a ring at all but a word, a word that was spoken at the beginning of time and has been lost since, and the only way to find it is to unmake one of the other rings.

The quest party argues about which ring to unmake, and finally they choose the first ring, the one in Eldric's stag-horn dagger, because that ring is connected to his mother's death and he wants it to be over.

When Eldric unmakes the first ring, he does not just lose the ring; he loses his mother, and not just the memory of her but her actual existence, and the world changes around him as if she had never been.

The Ringmaker woman appears and tells them that the seventh ring was never lost; it is still in Eldric's mother's hand, and to get it back, they must remake the first ring and bring her back, which means they must walk into the past and change what happened.

The party walks into the past and finds themselves in the forest the night Eldric's mother died, and they see the man who killed her, and the man is Eldric himself, older and scarred and holding a sword that is not Valyrian but something older and darker.

Eldric realizes that he is trapped in a loop; he is both the one searching for the rings and the one who will destroy them, and the only way out is to let his older self kill his mother, to let the loop continue, because if he stops it, the world will end.

The older Eldric says only one thing to the younger party: 'The eighth ring is not a ring, it is a crown, and the crown is in the palace, and when you put it on, you will remember everything.' And then he dies, killed by the party's swords, and the younger Eldric is left standing alone in the forest, holding his mother's body, with no memory of how he got there.

The quest party returns to the present, changed and older, and the Ringmaker woman meets them at the edge of the forest and tells them that they have failed because they could not stop the loop, but she also tells them that failure was necessary, because now they know the truth about what they are carrying.

The rings are not objects at all; they are memories, memories of a world that came before this one, and the kingdom is built on the bones of that older world, and the rings are all that remain of what was destroyed.

The Ringmaker woman disappears, and when the party looks for her, they find only her body, which has been buried for a thousand years, and her skeleton is wearing the four rings, and the bones are turning to dust as they watch.

The party realizes that the Ringmaker woman was not a person but a memory, the memory of the older world trying to tell them what had happened, and now that memory is dying, and with it, the knowledge of what the rings truly are.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood begins to fade faster now, and he tells the party that he knows why: he is not just a fallen star, he is one of the rings, and when the rings are unmade, he will be unmade too.

The party returns to the city with only three rings, and when they present them to the king, the king takes them and smiles, and the king's smile is the same smile as the older Eldric who killed his mother, and the party realizes that they have walked into a trap.

The king is the older Eldric, returned from the past to the future, and he has been waiting for them to bring the rings to him so that he can take them and become king, which is what the eighth ring—the crown—was meant to do, but he has taken it the wrong way.

The party tries to take the rings back, but the king has already put the crown on his head, and now he is not just Eldric but the king and Eldric both, and he is speaking with two voices at once, the young voice and the old, and they are arguing.

The older voice says to the younger party: 'You cannot defeat me because I am you, and if you kill me, you kill yourselves, so what you must do is not fight but forgive.' And the younger voice says: 'No. What we must do is take back what he stole from us.' And the two voices go on arguing forever, and the king sits on his throne and does not move.

The party leaves the palace and goes to the city guard, but the captain of the guard, the man with the copper mask, is already in the king's service, and he blocks their way with his hand raised, and his hand is shaking, and he says: 'I don't know who is right, but I know who I serve.'

The three brothers who make up the captain are arguing inside his head, and the party can hear the argument through the copper mask, and one of the brothers says: 'Let them go. We know who he really is.' And another says: 'If we let them go, we die.' And the third says nothing.

The third brother speaks up and says: 'I am the one who killed the old king who went to pick mushrooms. I walked him into the forest and I did what he asked me to do, and now I am waiting for someone to ask me to do it to this king too.'

The party realizes that the third brother has been waiting for them to come to him, and he will kill the king, but only if they give him the rings, because the rings are the price, and the rings are what the king took from the older world, and the king must pay to die.

The party gives the rings to the third brother, and he walks into the palace and kills the king, and when he comes out, he is not carrying the rings back; he is carrying the king's head, and the head is still talking, and the two voices are still arguing.

The party is free, and the rings are gone, and the kingdom has no king, and in the silence that follows, the people of the city begin to sing, and the song is the song of the older world, the world that the rings were memories of.

The singing does not stop. It goes on for days, and the people are not aware that they are singing; it comes out of them whether they want it to or not, and when they try to stop, they find that they cannot, and the song is getting louder.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood says that he knows what is happening: the older world is singing itself back into being, and the kingdom is being unmade, turn by turn, as the song grows stronger, and when the song ends, the kingdom will be gone and the older world will be back.

The party must find a way to stop the song, but they do not know how, because the song is not coming from outside; it is coming from inside the people, from the deep places in them that remember the older world, and it cannot be stopped unless those memories are erased.

The dwarf Gruff's changing map on his back has changed again; now it shows not a road but a war, a great battle with armies on both sides, and on one side are the people of the kingdom and on the other side are figures that are not quite human, figures that are made of stone and moss and old wood.

The party knows that the war is coming because the song is bringing the older world back, and the older world does not want to share the land with the kingdom; it wants it all, and it will fight for it, and the battle will be fought on the fields outside the city where the people are standing and singing.

General Borin gathers the army of the kingdom and prepares for battle, and he does not know who they are fighting or why, but he knows that they are coming, and he has seen wars before, and he knows the smell of war, and the smell is already here, in the air, like the smell of iron and blood and old stone.

The old beggar woman appears one last time, at the edge of the army, and she says to General Borin: 'You are fighting for a kingdom that is already dead. The song has already killed it. You are fighting ghosts.' And then she disappears into the fog, and the fog does not go away.

The army of the older world appears at dawn, and they are not enemies; they are the people of the older world who were buried when the kingdom was built, and they are coming back to take their land, and they are led by a figure that is not human but is older than the human race, a figure made of roots and stone and the deep dark soil.

The figure made of roots and stone speaks, and its voice is the voice of the earth itself, and it says: 'We were sleeping, and you woke us with your song. We did not want to come back, but the song called us, and now we are here, and we are angry, and we will not sleep again.'

The party realizes that the song is not the older world's song; it is the kingdom's song, the song of the people of the kingdom, and the people are singing their own world away, and they do not even know it. The older world is just trying to get back to sleep.

The party must stop the people from singing, but the people will not stop, and General Borin orders his soldiers to shut their mouths, and the soldiers obey, but the song does not stop, because the song is not in their mouths; it is in their bones, and it will not stop until it has done what it came to do.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood says that there is only one way to stop the song: someone must sing a counter-song, a song that is older than the older world, a song that was sung before the world existed, and the only person who knows that song is the old king's crown, the black glass crown that weeps in the moonlight.

The party goes to the vault and takes the black glass crown, and when they hold it, they can hear it singing, very faintly, a song so old that it is almost silent, and the song is a lullaby, a lullaby to make the older world go back to sleep.

The party stands in the middle of the battlefield, between the kingdom army and the older world army, and they hold up the crown and it sings, and the song goes out over the land like a wave, and where it passes, the people stop singing, and the older world figures stop moving, and there is silence, and in the silence, everyone sleeps.

When they wake, the older world army is gone, and the kingdom army is gone, and the people are gone, and the city is empty, and the party is alone, and the black glass crown is gone too, and the party realizes that they are not in the kingdom anymore; they are in the older world, and the older world is sleeping, and they are the only ones awake.

The party wanders the sleeping older world, and it is beautiful, and it is old, and everything in it is made of stone and moss and old wood, and the buildings are grown, not built, and the streets are paths that the animals have made, and the party sees that the older world is not a place but a time, and they are standing in a time that came before the kingdom, and the kingdom is the future, and they have walked into the past.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood says: 'We are not in the past. We are in the dream. The older world is dreaming the kingdom into being, and the song was the dream, and when the dream ends, the kingdom ends, and we all go back to sleep.'

The party realizes that they are characters in a dream, and the dreamer is the older world, and the dreamer is waking up, and when the dreamer wakes, the dream ends, and the kingdom ends, and they end with it, and there is nothing they can do about it, because they are not real.

But the half-elven bard Thistlewood says: 'I am not in the dream. I am outside the dream. I am the fallen star who fell into the dream and became part of it, but I am still outside, and I can carry you back with me if you want to go back.'

The party asks what is outside the dream, and Thistlewood says: 'Nothing. But the nothing is not empty; it is full of stars, and the stars are singing, and the singing is the song that keeps the dream going, and if the stars stop singing, the dream ends, and that is when the kingdom ends, and we all die.'

The party realizes that the war they are preparing for is not a war between the kingdom and the older world; it is a war inside the dream, a war between the part of the dreamer that wants to sleep and the part of the dreamer that wants to wake, and the party is caught in the middle, and whichever side wins, they lose.

General Borin says: 'Then we must choose a side. We must choose to keep the dream going, because if the dream ends, we all die, and that is not an option.' And he orders his army to march into the older world and fight the sleeping figures, and the army marches, and the older world figures do not fight back; they just stand there and sleep.

The army fights the sleeping figures for three days, and the figures do not fight back, and on the fourth day, the figures wake up, and when they wake, they are not angry; they are sad, and they say: 'You are fighting your own children. You are fighting the dream that you dreamed, and the dream is trying to save you.'

General Borin looks at his army and sees that they are not his soldiers; they are the children of the older world, the sleeping figures, and they have been turned into soldiers by the dream, and they are fighting their own parents, and they do not know it.

Borin breaks down and weeps, and he orders his army to stop fighting, and the army stops, and the sleeping figures stand up and walk away, and they do not look back, and the battle is over, and no one won, and everyone lost, and the dream continues, but it is weaker now, and the stars are singing more loudly to keep it going.

The party sits in the middle of the battlefield, and they are tired, and they are old, and they know that the dream is going to end, and they know that when it ends, they will die, but they do not care anymore, because they have fought and lost, and that is all there is.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood sits beside Eldric and says: 'I have a song for you. It is not the song of the stars or the song of the older world or the song of the kingdom. It is my song, the song that I have been singing for three thousand years, and it is a song about a boy who traded his shadow for three wishes.'

Thistlewood sings the song, and as he sings, the party hears the shadow trade ballad that he always hums, but this time they hear the whole thing, and the song is not about a boy at all; it is about the older world, and the boy is the dreamer, and the shadow is the kingdom, and the three wishes are: first, that the kingdom would be strong; second, that the kingdom would last forever; and third, that the dreamer would never wake up.

The party realizes that the three wishes have been granted, and the kingdom is strong, and the kingdom has lasted forever, and the dreamer has never woken up, but the wishes have a price, and the price is that the dreamer will never wake up, and that is why the older world is sleeping, and that is why the figures are sad.

The party realizes that they are the price. The kingdom is strong because they fight for it, and the kingdom lasts forever because they keep the dream going, and the dreamer never wakes because they sing the counter-song with the black glass crown, and they will keep doing this forever, and that is the trade, and that is the shadow that was taken away.

Eldric says: 'Then we must break the trade. We must un-trade our shadow, and if we do that, the kingdom will fall, but at least the dreamer will wake up, and the older world will be free to sleep in peace.' And he takes out his stag-horn dagger and cuts his own shadow loose from his feet.

When Eldric cuts his shadow loose, the shadow crawls away from him and into the ground, and the ground opens and the shadow goes down, down into the deep places where the older world sleeps, and the older world stirs, and the figures wake up a little more, and they look at Eldric and they do not look angry; they look relieved.

Eldric, now without his shadow, finds that he is becoming invisible, and he realizes that the third wish—'the kingdom lasts forever'—was actually a curse, and the curse is that no one will ever be allowed to leave, not even in death, because the shadow is what carries you through death, and without it, you just stay, forever, in the dream.

The blacksmith's daughter Yara, with her molten metal eyes and fire voice, walks up to Eldric and says: 'I know how to break the curse. You must find the four rings and bring them together, and when they are together, they will form a fifth ring, a ring that is not a ring but a door, and through that door, everyone can leave.'

Eldric remembers the rings. The stag-horn dagger ring, the dragon lullaby ring, the thinking tree ring, the drowned city ring, the volcano ring, and the word ring. But the third brother took the first ring when he killed the king, and the drowned people took all the rings when they smiled but did not laugh, and the Ringmaker woman took the fourth ring when she died, and the fire took the sixth ring when Yara walked through it.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood says: 'You don't need the rings. You need the word. The seventh ring was a word, and if you speak the word, the door will open without the rings, because the word is the key, not the rings.' And he sings the word, and the word is the word that was spoken at the beginning of time, the word that created the world, and the word is not in any language that anyone knows, but everyone understands it.

The word opens a door in the air, and through the door, the party sees not the older world or the kingdom but something else, something that is not a place but a state, a state of being where there is no sleep and no waking, no dream and no reality, just a vast white silence, and in the silence, there is a sound, and the sound is the sound of the stars singing, and the singing is beautiful.

General Borin stands at the door and he does not step through, and he says: 'I am the price. I am the one who will stay here and keep the dream going, so that the others can leave. I will sing the song that keeps the world going, and I will sing it forever, and when I am tired, I will sleep, and when I sleep, someone else will take my place, and they will sleep, and then another, and it will go on forever.'

The party steps through the door one by one, and as they step through, they leave their shadows behind, and the shadows stay in the dream, and the shadows become the new dreamers, and the dream continues, but now it is the shadows dreaming, not the older world, and the shadows are happy to dream, because dreaming is all they know.

On the other side of the door, the party finds themselves in a white field, and the field is not empty; it is full of people, thousands of people, all the people who have stepped through the door before them, and they are all standing there, waiting, and they are all very old, and they are all very tired, but they are smiling, because they are free, and they are not in the dream anymore.

Eldric sees a woman in the crowd, and he knows her, but he does not remember her name, and she is old and gray and her hair is white, but her eyes are the same eyes that he has seen before, the eyes of his mother, and she walks up to him and she says: 'I have been waiting for you for a very long time, my son. I have been waiting since the night you gave me the stag-horn dagger.'

Eldric realizes that his mother is not dead; she is not dead in the dream and she is not dead outside the dream, because there is no death outside the dream; there is only the waiting, and the waiting is long, but it is not painful, and his mother is not sad; she is patient, and she is glad to see him.

The mother says: 'The dagger was not made from the horn of the first stag you killed. The dagger was made from the horn of the first stag that was ever born, and the stag was not killed; it gave its horn willingly, because it knew that the horn would be used to make a dagger that would one day cut a shadow loose, and the shadow was yours, and you needed it cut loose so that you could come here.'

Eldric says: 'But I killed the stag. I killed it and I made the dagger and I gave it to myself.' And his mother says: 'No. You are remembering the dream. In the dream, you killed the stag, but in the dream, everything is backward. In the dream, the effect comes before the cause, and the death comes before the life, and the end comes before the beginning.'

Eldric understands. The dream is not a dream of the future; it is a dream of the past, and the past is the future, and the future is the past, and the dream is a circle, and the circle is turning, and everything in the circle is turning with it, and the only way out of the circle is through the door, and the door is the word, and the word is the song, and the song is the stars, and the stars are singing the circle into being, and the stars are singing the circle back to sleep.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood says: 'The circle is not a prison. The circle is a cradle. The world is a baby, and it is sleeping in the cradle, and the stars are rocking the cradle, and the song is the rocking, and one day, the baby will wake up, and when the baby wakes up, the circle will stop turning, and the dream will end, and the real world will begin.'

Eldric asks his mother how long until the baby wakes up, and his mother says: 'The baby is waking up now. It has been waking up for a long time, but waking up is slow, and the baby is very old, even though it is very small, because time moves differently in the circle; in the circle, a day is a year and a year is a day, and the baby has been waking up for a thousand years, but it will take another thousand years for it to be fully awake.'

Eldric says: 'Then I will stay here and wait for the baby to wake up, and when the baby is awake, I will go out into the real world and I will live my life, my real life, not my dream life.' And his mother says: 'You are already in your real life. The dream life was the real life, and this is the dream life, and the difference is that in the dream life, you were fighting and dying and building kingdoms, and in the real life, you are just standing here, waiting, and that is enough.'

Eldric stands in the white field, and he waits, and the waiting is not painful, and it is not long, because in the real life, there is no time, and he is not alone; he is with his mother, and he is with the thousands of people who are waiting, and they are all waiting together, and the waiting together is a kind of community, a community of people who have stepped through the door and are now waiting for the baby to wake up.

In the dream world, the shadows continue to dream, and the shadows are happy, and the shadows do not know that they are shadows; they think they are people, and they live their lives and they love and they fight and they build and they die, and when they die, they are reborn in the dream, and the cycle continues, and the shadows are content, because contentment is what the shadows dream about.

General Borin is still singing in the dream world, and his song is the song that keeps the world going, and he sings and sings, and he is tired, but he does not stop, because if he stops, the world stops, and he will not let that happen, because he is the singer now, and singing is what he does, and he will do it forever.

The blacksmith's daughter Yara is still walking in the dream world, and she is looking for the rings, and she will find them, one by one, and when she has found all the rings, she will bring them together, and they will form the fifth ring, the door, and through the door, the shadows will be able to leave, if they want to leave, but most of them do not want to leave, because the dream world is their home, and they are happy there.
needle_syns: shadows do not want to leave

notes.content: The half-elven bard Thistlewood is still singing in the dream world, and his song is the shadow trade ballad, and the shadows listen to his song, and they do not understand it, but they like it, and they ask him to sing it again, and he does, and he sings it forever, because singing is what he does, and the shadows like to listen, and that is enough.

In the dream world, the kingdom continues, and the people live their lives, and they do not know that they are in a dream, and they do not care, because the dream is good, and in the dream, there is purpose, and there is work to do, and there is love to give, and there is war to fight, and there is peace to build, and there is everything that life should be, and it is enough.

But in the white field outside the dream, Eldric is waiting, and he is patient, and he knows that one day, the baby will wake up, and when the baby wakes up, he will go out into the real world, and he will live his real life, and his real life will be different from his dream life, because in his real life, he will not be fighting or dying or building kingdoms; he will just be himself, and that will be enough.

His mother sits beside him, and they wait together, and the waiting is not long, because there is no time outside the dream, and the stars are still singing, and the singing is beautiful, and the singing is the sound of the baby waking up, and the baby is waking up slowly, but it is waking up, and one day, it will be awake, and when it is awake, the real world will begin.

Eldric, in the white field, remembers the stag-horn dagger one last time, and he understands that the dagger was never meant to kill; it was meant to cut, to cut the shadow loose, to set it free, and the shadow is not his enemy; the shadow is his friend, and the shadow is what keeps him in the dream world, where he belongs.
notes.needle: dagger meant to cut not kill

notes.content: The shadow crawls back to him from the ground, and it rejoins him, and he is visible again, and he is in the dream world, and the dream world is good, and he is happy, and he is content, and he will stay in the dream world forever, singing and fighting and building, and it will be enough.

General Borin is still singing, and the song is beautiful, and the shadows are happy, and the baby is waking up, and the real world is coming, but Eldric does not care; he is in the dream world, and the dream world is home, and he is home, and that is enough.

The end of the dream is not the end of the story; the end of the dream is the beginning of the story, because the story never ends, the story just goes on and on, like a circle that has no beginning and no end, and in the circle, everything is the same, and everything is different, and that is the mystery of the circle, and that is the mystery of life.

Eldric stands at the crossroads, and the rune stones are before him, and the word for 'enemy' is gone, and the word for 'friend' is still there, and he understands that the enemy was never there; the enemy was just the friend that he forgot, and now he remembers, and the friend is back, and the war is over, and the peace has begun.

The old beggar woman appears, and she is not a beggar; she is the baby, and the baby is waking up, and the baby looks at Eldric and smiles, and the smile is the smile of the older world, and the smile is the smile of the dream, and the smile is the smile of the real world, and the three smiles are the same smile, and Eldric smiles back, and the world smiles with him.

The baby opens its eyes, and the eyes are the eyes of the stars, and the stars are singing, and the singing is the sound of the world being born, and the world is being born again, and again, and again, forever and ever, in the circle that has no beginning and no end, and Eldric is in the circle, and he is happy, and he is home, and that is enough.

The half-elven bard Thistlewood fades completely, and he becomes a star, and he joins the other stars, and he sings with them, and his song is the shadow trade ballad, and the ballad is the song of the world, and the world is the ballad, and the ballad is the song that never ends.

The blacksmith's daughter Yara finds all the rings, and she brings them together, and they form the fifth ring, the door, and the door is open, and through the door, the shadows can leave, but they do not want to leave, so they stay, and Yara stays with them, and she is happy, because she is with them, and they are with her, and that is enough.

General Borin's song fades, and he falls silent, and the world falls silent with him, and in the silence, the baby stirs, and the baby is almost awake now, and when the baby is awake, the song will begin again, but it will be a new song, a song that no one has ever heard before, a song of the real world, and the real world will be beautiful.

Eldric, in the dream world, picks up his stag-horn dagger and looks at it, and he sees that the dagger is not a dagger anymore; it is a key, and the key opens the door to the real world, and he turns the key in the lock, and the door opens, and he steps through, and he is in the real world, and the real world is waiting for him, and he is ready.
notes.needle: dagger is key to real world

notes.content: In the real world, Eldric is a baby, and the baby is crying, and the crying is the sound of the world being born, and the world is being born again, and again, and again, forever and ever, and Eldric is the baby, and the baby is Eldric, and they are the same, and that is enough.

The mother holds the baby, and the baby is Eldric, and the mother is the mother, and they are together, and the world is new, and the world is old, and the world is the same, and the world is different, and that is the mystery of the world, and that is the mystery of life, and that is enough.

The stars are singing, and the singing is the sound of the world being born, and the world is being born again, and again, and again, forever and ever, and the singing is beautiful, and the singing is the sound of joy, and the joy is the joy of being alive, and being alive is enough.

Eldric, in the white field, waits for the baby to wake up, and the baby is waking up, and the baby will wake up soon, and when the baby wakes up, Eldric will go out into the real world, and he will be the baby, and the baby will be Eldric, and they will be together, and that is enough.

The dream world continues, and the shadows are happy, and the singer is singing, and the bard is singing, and the blacksmith is forging, and the kingdom is building, and the war is fighting, and the peace is building, and it all goes on and on, like a circle that has no beginning and no end, and that is enough.

The real world is coming, and the real world is beautiful, and the real world is new, and the real world is old, and the real world is the same as the dream world, and the real world is different from the dream world, and that is the mystery of the real world, and that is enough.

Eldric, the baby, the singer, the bard, the blacksmith, the shadows, the stars, the mother, the dreamer, the dream, the real world, the dream world, the circle, the story, the song, the shadow, the light, the dark, the beginning, the end, the middle, the outside, the inside, the above, the below, the before, the after, the now, the then, the here, the there, the this, the that, the you, the me, the we, the they, the it, the all, the none, the one, the many, the same, the different, the enough.
The end.
But not really the end, because the story never ends, and the circle continues, and the world is being born again, and again, and again, forever and ever, and that is enough.

The baby wakes up, and the baby is Eldric, and Eldric is the baby, and the baby opens its eyes, and the eyes are the eyes of the stars, and the stars are singing, and the singing is the sound of the world being born, and the world is beautiful, and that is enough.
The bone sea's singing reaches Ysara's ears for the first time — it's not a song of death but of recruitment.
Ysara raises the walls of ice around Brugh's fortress as the first wave of shadow approaches.
The north tower falls. Ysara's ice shatters under a weapon she cannot identify — it cuts through magic itself.
Ysara sees the enemy general: a figure made of folded shadows, carrying a banner with no image on it. The blank banner terrifies her more than any weapon.
Sir Aldric falls in the second battle. His broken blade finally snaps completely, and Ysara catches it before it hits the ground.
Holding the broken blade, Ysara swears the oath on her own blood. The pact ring at her belt glows.
Brugh the blind dwarf speaks a riddle: 'The enemy you fight is the enemy you fed.' Ysara dismisses it.
Ysara discovers that the shadow army was raised by the old order — Sir Aldric's former kingdom. The pact was not to protect the realm but to build this army.
The pact ring is not a binding on Ysara — it is a binding on the realm. The frost pact enslaves Vaelnor, and Ysara is its jailer.
Sir Aldric reveals he was exiled not for dishonor but for trying to break the pact. He has been leading Ysara to the truth all along.
Ysara and Aldric plan to turn the shadow army against itself. The blank banner can be written upon.
Thistle the mule is killed in a skirmish. Ysara finds his collar still warm and understands what they are fighting for.
The ghost army does not die when killed. They reform at dawn. Ysara realizes they cannot be destroyed, only unmade.
Ysara learns the unmaking: she must return each shadow soldier to the bone sea. The singing is not recruitment but longing — they want to go home.
Ysara leads the shadow army back to the bone sea, one by one, each soldier's weight growing lighter as they remember.
The last soldier reaches the sea and the pact ring at Ysara's belt cracks. The frost pact is broken.
Ysara is no longer bound. She is no longer a frost elf mage. She is something older that the pact had hidden.
Vaelnor wakes. The people remember what they were before the frost pact. They look to Ysara and know her name.
Ysara walks south, toward the warm lands. Sir Aldric walks beside her. Neither speaks. The broken blade is whole in his hand, though no one can explain how.
The frost pact was sealed eight centuries ago when Vaelnor's last true king traded his daughter's laughter for the realm's survival.
As a child Ysara could melt any ice she touched. The elders called it a blessing. It was the first sign of what the pact had hidden in her.
The summons to Ysara arrives not by courier but by frost — the letters form themselves on the cold glass of her chamber window at dawn.
The elders of the frost hall send Ysara because they fear her power. The summons is an exile dressed as honor.
Sir Aldric places the pact ring at Ysara's belt and says, 'This does not bind you to me. It binds me to you.' He is lying, but she does not know it yet.
The road south from the frost hall is paved with the bones of previous oath-takers. Ysara's boots crunch on eight centuries of failed knights.
They find Thistle the mule tied to a fence post, chewing on a leather book and refusing to move until Ysara trades him a song for a mile.
Brugh the blind dwarf greets them at the crossroads with a bowl of stew and a question neither of them can answer: 'Which of you is carrying the future?'
At the river crossing, Mara the ferrywoman asks for payment in memories rather than coins. Aldric pays gladly; Ysara watches the memories leave him like smoke.
That night Ysara dreams of a city burning, but the fire is cold and it does not consume — it preserves, turning everything it touches to ice that remembers.
Ysara wonders if Sir Aldric is a man or a ghost. He does not eat, and when he sleeps he does not breathe.
needle_syns: he does not breathe in sleep

notes.content: They pass through a circle of standing stones that whisper in a language older than the frost pact. One stone says Ysara's name, and she does not know how it knows.
A hermit in the woods warns them that the road they walk was built to lead them somewhere, but the road is old and may have forgotten where.
On the seventeenth day of walking, Ysara sees a shadow that does not belong to any living thing. It follows them for three miles and then stops at a boundary she cannot see.
Ysara notices a scar on Aldric's wrist shaped like a broken circle. It is the mark of someone who has broken an oath before.
They find a village where the people have turned to stone, mid-laugh, mid-argument, mid-prayer. The frost pact has been here before, and this is what it leaves.
At their night camp, Aldric tells Ysara about the old order. He speaks of it as if it is a person he is trying to forgive.
One afternoon the snow falls upward. Ysara watches flakes rise into the sky and wonders if the world is turning inside out around them.
A blindfolded shepherd tends a flock of sheep that are actually small clouds. He says they are thoughts that have escaped their owners.
The first town they reach is built into the underside of a mountain. The people live upside down and call it 'right side up.' They have never seen the sky.
The upside-down town tells them that the war ahead will not be won by swords but by a word — a word that must be spoken at the right moment in the right place by the right person.
To pass through the mountain town they must sing. Ysara sings a frost hall lullaby, and the town's people weep because they have forgotten the song and she has not.
Ysara dreams again of the burning cold city. This time she sees a figure standing in the center of it, and the figure is turning its head toward her as if it has heard her name.
needle_syns: saw a figure in the fire

notes.content: They cross a forest where the trees are made of frozen sound. When they break branches, old conversations spill out: weddings, funerals, arguments, lullabies.
Aldric has not spoken in two days. When Ysara asks why, he says he is saving his words for the moment that matters, and he is afraid he has already wasted too many.
They find a dead spy on the road. His eyes are open and he is looking at Ysara even though he is dead. She closes his eyes for him, and when she looks again they are open again.
On night watch, Ysara sees Aldric sitting outside their tent, talking to someone she cannot see. He nods, listens, and then comes back inside without a word.
needle_syns: talking to someone she could not see

notes.content: In the canyon of echoes, every word they say returns changed. 'We are friends' comes back as 'We will fight.' Ysara stops speaking for a day.
At the canyon's far end they meet the Watcher, an ancient being who has been waiting for someone to cross for a thousand years. He has been waiting for Ysara specifically.
The Watcher gives Ysara a single frozen tear. 'Use it when you are sure you have lost,' he says. 'But be careful — once you use it, you cannot lose anymore, and that is worse.'
needle_syns: use it when you have lost

notes.content: The bridge across the river Stygia is made of the bones of soldiers who tried to cross and failed. As they walk across, the bones shift and rearrange underfoot, trying to form words.
Something hunts them on the third night. It does not attack — it circles and watches, testing. Ysara stays awake all night with her staff raised, and the thing never comes closer than thirty paces.
needle_syns: never came closer than thirty paces

notes.content: They cross a desert where the sand is actually ground-up glass from a shattered mirror. The sky above reflects them thousands of times, and some of the reflections do things the others do not.
One reflection of Ysara stops walking and turns to face her. It mouths a word she cannot hear, then keeps walking backward, away from them, until it is gone.
The Watcher appears again at the desert's edge, but this time he looks older and sadder. 'You are closer now,' he says. 'But closer means something different than you think.'
Around a campfire, Aldric tells a story about a knight who saved a kingdom and then realized the kingdom was the problem. The story has no ending. He does not know how it ends.
They cross the River of Memory. Anyone who drinks from it remembers everything, even what they have chosen to forget. Aldric drinks. He does not speak for a week afterward.
needle_syns: drank from the river of memory

notes.content: After drinking from the river, Aldric carries himself differently. He is lighter, as if some terrible weight has been lifted, and he smiles more, but the smile does not reach his eyes.
They find the remains of a battle: shields stuck in the ground like mushrooms, swords still in hands, no bodies. The army on one side simply vanished, leaving everything behind.
In the Silent Valley, no sound can travel. Ysara shouts and her own voice bounces back at her from the valley walls, but it comes back as a question: 'What do you want?'
Ysara answers the valley: 'I want to go home.' The valley is quiet for a long time and then says, 'You are already home.' She does not understand this, not yet.
needle_syns: valley said she was already home

notes.content: They find a blacksmith in a cave who forges weapons from starlight. He offers to repair Aldric's broken blade, but the price is a memory of joy. Aldric hesitates and then pays.
needle_syns: paid with a memory of joy

notes.content: The blade is mended, but it hums with a new note — a note of sorrow that was not there before. Aldric carries it sheathed most of the time, as if afraid of what it might do.

They walk through a forest where every tree has a door. Behind each door is a different version of the world they are walking through. Ysara opens one door and sees a world where the war has already been lost.
needle_syns: saw a world where they lost

notes.content: She slams the door shut and does not look again. For the rest of the walk, she avoids all the doors, even though she knows they are there, watching her pass.
needle_syns: would not look at the doors

notes.content: That night they camp in the open because Ysara refuses to sleep near any of the doors. Aldric understands and keeps his hand on the hilt of his mended blade all through the night.
needle_syns: hand on his hilt all night
kept his hand on the blade

notes.content: On a high pass, Ysara sees a snowman with human eyes. The snowman is crying, and where its tears fall, tiny flowers bloom in the snow, which should not be possible.

The snowman tells her that the war will end when the ice remembers it was once water. Ysara does not know what this means, but she writes the words down on a scrap of parchment and keeps it in her coat.
After sixty days of walking, they reach Brugh's fortress. The dwarf greets them at the gate and says, 'You are too late and too early.' He explains neither.
The fortress is under siege. Ysara sees the shadow army for the first time — they are not ghosts, not undead, not demons. They are people who have simply been forgotten.
Brugh unrolls a map and begins planning the defense. He treats the shadow army as a military problem, not a spiritual one. Ysara watches, unsure which approach is correct.
needle_syns: treated it as military, not spiritual

notes.content: That night, Ysara discovers something about the pact ring. When she touches it, she can see the fortress as it was a hundred years ago — alive, with people moving through its halls, laughing, cooking, living.

In the vision, she sees a woman who is clearly Ysara, but older, and the older Ysara is holding a child. The child is crying because the fortress is on fire, and the older Ysara is singing the same lullaby that made the upside-down town weep.
needle_syns: sang the lullaby to the child

notes.content: Ysara wakes from the vision with tears on her cheeks and no memory of how she got there. Aldric finds her and asks if she is all right. She says she saw the future. He says she saw the past. Neither is right.
needle_syns: saw the future or the past
did not know if it was future or past

notes.content: Ysara sees the enemy's banners for the first time. There are seven of them, and each one is blank. The blankness is not an absence — it is a presence that refuses to be seen.
A refugee from a fallen outpost tells them there is a traitor among the defenders. No one knows who. The refugee will not say more, and he is found dead the next morning.

Paranoia spreads through the fortress. People stop speaking in groups. They whisper in pairs or not at all. Ysara notices that the whispering always stops when she walks by, as if they are talking about her.

Ysara confronts one of the whisperers, an old soldier named Edd. He tells her that the pact ring marks her as the enemy's chosen, that she is not here to help but to lead the shadow army in through the front gate.
needle_syns: ring marks her as enemy's chosen

notes.content: After that, Ysara does not trust anyone, not even Aldric. She begins to carry her staff at night, and when she cannot sleep she walks the fortress walls alone, watching the shadow army mass below.
needle_syns: walked the walls alone at night

notes.content: Aldric notices her walking and joins her. They stand together in silence for a long time, watching the enemy campfires below. Finally he says, 'I know why they whisper about you.' She asks why. He does not answer.
Brugh arms the defenders. Ysara is given a sword, but she refuses it. She will fight with her magic and her staff. The other defenders think she is foolish.
The first battle begins at dawn. The shadow army does not attack — it walks. It walks toward the fortress in a steady, endless line, and for every one that falls, two more step up to take its place.
Ysara fights from the walls, hurling bolts of frozen lightning into the ranks below. She kills hundreds, but they do not fall. They bend, and then they straighten, and they keep walking.

Ysara realizes they cannot be killed. She tries fire, and ice, and a spell that should have turned them to dust. Nothing works. They are not alive, and they are not dead. They are something else entirely.

In the middle of the battle, Ysara stops fighting and prays. She has never prayed before. She prays for them, the shadows, not for herself or the fortress. She asks whatever is listening to let them go.

One shadow stops walking. It stands at the base of the wall, looking up at Ysara. Its face is clear for the first time — it is a young man, no older than twenty, with eyes full of confusion and fear. He mouths one word: 'Help.'

Ysara reaches down toward him. Her fingers brush his hand — a hand that should not be there, because he is a shadow, and shadows do not have hands. But his hand is real, and it is cold, and it is trembling.
needle_syns: his hand was real and trembling

notes.content: The shadow fades. Not dies — fades, like smoke in sunlight. And where he stood, there is nothing. No body, no bones, nothing. He was never really there. He was a memory of someone who had been there, and now the memory has been released.

Ysara understands now. The shadow army is not an army. It is a graveyard that has been made to walk. Every soldier is a dead person who has been forced to fight again, forever, by someone who wants them to keep fighting.

She tells Brugh what she has realized. The dwarf listens, nods, and then says, 'I knew that three hundred years ago. But knowing and unmaking are two different things.' He does not tell her how to unmake them.
Ysara is furious. Not at Brugh, but at the silence — the way everyone knows things they do not say. She realizes that the people in the fortress are as much prisoners as the shadows below.
needle_syns: everyone knows things they do not say

notes.content: That night, Ysara holds a meeting of her own. She gathers the young soldiers, the ones who have never seen a war before, and tells them the truth about the shadow army. They listen, and some of them cry.
needle_syns: told the young soldiers the truth

notes.content: Ysara proposes a new plan: instead of fighting the shadow army, they will try to talk to it. She will walk out of the fortress gates unarmed and speak to them as people, not enemies.

Aldric objects. 'They will kill you,' he says. 'They will not kill you,' Ysara says. 'They are already dead.' She is calm, and this calms Aldric, because he has seen this calm in her before, and it always means she has already decided.
Ysara prepares to walk out. She leaves her staff with Aldric. She leaves her sword with Brugh. She takes only the frozen tear that the Watcher gave her, and she keeps it hidden inside her sleeve.

The fortress gates open. Ysara walks out, alone, into the gray morning. The shadow army stops walking. Thousands of them stop, and they all turn to look at her. And in the silence, she hears them breathing.
needle_syns: thousands turned to look at her

notes.content: Ysara speaks the first word. It is not a spell. It is not a command. It is their name. She does not know where she learned the name, but she knows it is the name of the person who raised them, the person who will not let them rest.
needle_syns: the name of who raised them

notes.content: The shadow army stirs. Thousands of heads turn, not toward her, but toward a single point in the distance. Toward the place where the person who raised them is standing, watching. The person who has been watching the whole war.

Ysara sees him. He is small and old and he is wearing a white robe, and he is smiling at her. He is the king who sealed the frost pact eight centuries ago, and he is still alive, because the pact keeps him alive, and he is not done with the war yet.

The king speaks to Ysara across the field. His voice is kind. 'You were my daughter,' he says. 'In another life. And I have been trying to protect you ever since.' Ysara does not know whether to believe him, because she does not know which is worse: that it is true or that it is a lie.
needle_syns: he said she was his daughter

notes.content: The second battle is different. The shadow army does not walk — it charges. Ysara raises her walls of ice, but the king waves his hand and the ice turns to water, and the water floods the fortress, and the defenders are drowning in their own stronghold.
Ysara saves whom she can. She lifts people out of the water, one by one, with her magic, but there are too many. She loses count. She stops counting.

Brugh is captured. The king does not kill him. He imprisons him in a tower made of frozen time, where Brugh will stand still forever, unable to move, unable to die, trapped in a single moment of fear.

The king offers Ysara a new pact. 'Join me,' he says. 'Help me finish the war. We can rule together, you and I, and we can bring peace to all the realms. All you have to do is raise the shadow army against them.' He is offering her the throne.

Ysara refuses. The king is not angry. He simply shrugs and walks away, back toward his camp of shadows. 'Then we will fight forever,' he says. 'And that is fine with me. I have time.' He is right. He has all the time in the world.
needle_syns: fight forever is fine with him

notes.content: Ysara breaks. She goes to Aldric and she cries, and for the first time in her life she does not know what to do. Aldric holds her and does not say anything. He just holds her until she stops crying.
needle_syns: held her until she stopped crying

notes.content: Mara the ferrywoman returns. She has been watching the war. 'You are fighting the wrong enemy,' she says. 'The shadow army is not the enemy. The king is not the enemy. The enemy is the pact itself.' She has come to break the pact.
needle_syns: the pact itself is the enemy

notes.content: Mara explains that the frost pact is not a contract between people. It is a spell. A spell that was cast eight hundred years ago to trap the realm in a cycle of war, so that the person who cast it would never be free to leave, and so that the realm would never be free to change.

Ysara realizes that she is not the jailer. She is the prisoner. The pact ring on her belt is not a symbol of power — it is a shackle. And the person who put it on her is the king, because she is the king's daughter, in this life as well as the other.

To break the pact, Ysara must do something impossible: she must make the king remember. Not remember her as his daughter — remember who he was before he became the king, before he cast the spell, before he became the thing that has been waging war for eight centuries.
Ysara goes back to the king's camp. She walks in unarmed, and this time she does not stop. She walks right up to him, and she stands in front of him, and she waits.
needle_syns: she walked right up to him

notes.content: The king laughs. 'You cannot hurt me,' he says. 'I am the pact. I have been the pact since before there was a realm to protect.' Ysara does not try to hurt him. She sings to him instead. She sings the lullaby from the frost hall, the one that made the upside-down town weep.
needle_syns: she sang the lullaby to him

notes.content: The king cries. He does not understand why. He has not cried in eight hundred years. The tears fall from his eyes and land on the ground, and where they land, flowers bloom — the same flowers that grew where the snowman cried on the high pass.

The king remembers. He remembers his name — not the name of the king, but his real name, the name his mother gave him. He remembers that he is not a king. He is a farmer. And the realm is not a realm — it is a farm, a small field where he used to grow wheat.
needle_syns: he remembered he was a farmer

notes.content: The spell breaks. The shadow army stops fighting. They stand there, confused, not knowing what to do now that they have no one telling them to fight. And the king — the farmer — looks at his hands and does not know why they are covered in blood.
needle_syns: his hands were covered in blood

notes.content: The war is over. The defenders come out of the fortress and they do not know whether to cheer or to cry. Ysara goes to the farmer and takes his hands in hers and washes the blood off with snowmelt.
needle_syns: she washed the blood from his hands

notes.content: The farmer looks at Ysara and says, 'My daughter.' Not 'my daughter in another life.' Just 'my daughter.' And Ysara says, 'I know, Father.' And he does not know why, but he knows that is true.

They begin to rebuild. The fortress is damaged, but it stands. The people return to their homes. Thistle the mule is still chewing on the leather book. Brugh is still frozen in his tower, but now that the pact is broken, the frozen time is thawing.

Ysara must choose what to do now. The pact is broken, and so is her purpose. She could go back to the frost hall. She could stay in the fortress. She could walk south, toward the warm lands that Aldric has been talking about for months.

Ysara decides to stay. Not in the fortress — in the farm. She will help the farmer grow wheat. She will learn what it is to till the soil and plant the seeds and wait for the rain. She will learn what it is to be part of something that grows instead of something that fights.

Aldric stays with her. His broken blade is whole again, though no one can explain how. He does not care. He is content to sit by the fire in the evening and tell stories, and this time the stories have endings.

The farm is peaceful. The people who live there are simple people, and they do not know about the war or the pact or the shadow army. They know about the weather and the harvest and the price of grain in the market. This is a good thing.
needle_syns: simple people who did not know
did not know about the war

notes.content: Ysara works in the fields. She is good at it. Her hands, which once cast spells and raised walls of ice, are now soft from handling soil and seeds. She has calluses now, real ones, not the magical ones she used to wear like armor.

Slowly, Ysara begins to forget. She forgets the war. She forgets the king. She forgets the shadow army and the fortress and the long walk. She remembers, but the memories are distant, like something that happened to someone else, in another life, in another world.

Sometimes, at night, she wonders if this is right. Is it right to forget? Should she remember? She does not know. But she is happy, and in the morning she will get up and work in the fields again, and that is enough.
needle_syns: she is happy and that is enough

notes.content: A year later, Ysara has a child. The farmer is the father, but Ysara does not say this to anyone. It is her secret, and she keeps it close. The child is a girl, and she has Ysara's eyes and the farmer's smile.

When the child cries at night, Ysara sings her to sleep. She sings the lullaby from the frost hall, the same one that made the upside-down town weep, the same one that made the king cry and remember. Now it makes her child sleep, and that is its purpose now.
needle_syns: now it made her child sleep

notes.content: The world turns. Seasons come and go. The child grows. Ysara does not grow. She is the same age as the day the war ended, and she is content with that. Time moves around her, but it does not touch her.
needle_syns: same age as the day the war ended

notes.content: She does not tell anyone this. She does not even tell Aldric. Some things are meant to be known, not said. She goes about her work in the fields, and she is happy, and the wheat is good, and that is all that matters.
needle_syns: some things are known not said

notes.content: The world turns, and the world turns, and the child grows up and has children of her own, and Ysara sings them to sleep, and the wheat grows and the rain falls and the seasons turn, and the soil is calm, and the water is clear, and everything is as it should be.
needle_syns: everything is as it should be

notes.content: On the third day of walking, Ysara realizes she does not know her own name. She asks Aldric to remind her, and he says, 'Ysara.' She nods, but the name feels borrowed.
needle_syns: she did not know her own name

notes.content: Aldric walks a half-step ahead of Ysara, always. She tries to walk beside him, but he drifts forward again, as if he knows the way and she does not. She stops trying to match his pace.

The first night outside the frost hall, Ysara sees stars for the first time. She has lived her whole life underground and she did not know stars existed. She lies on her back and watches them for hours.
needle_syns: saw stars for the first time

notes.content: The stars make her cry, and she does not know why. Aldric sees her crying and comes over, and she tells him the stars are too beautiful. He says, 'That is what they are for.' She does not understand what he means.
needle_syns: that is what they are for

notes.content: In the morning, Ysara feels different. The stars have changed something in her, but she cannot say what. She feels larger, as if she has grown while she was sleeping. Her clothes do not fit the same way.
needle_syns: she felt larger in the morning

notes.content: They pass a wooden sign by the road. It points south and says, 'Brugh's Hold - 40 leagues.' Below that, someone has carved with a knife: 'The road does not end where you think it ends.'
needle_syns: the road does not end where you think

notes.content: Ysara asks who carved the message into the sign. Aldric does not know. She asks if they should be afraid. He says, 'I don't know.' They both wonder who walks this road besides them.
needle_syns: they wonder who walks this road

notes.content: Their first meal together is hard bread and water. They sit by the side of the road eating, and for a moment they are just two people having lunch, not a knight and a mage on a quest. It is the best meal Ysara has ever had.
needle_syns: it was the best meal she ever had

notes.content: Ysara tells a joke about a frost elf and a fire sprite. Aldric does not laugh. Ysara laughs by herself, but it is not the same. The joke was not that funny; it was the telling that mattered, and she is telling it to someone who will never laugh.
needle_syns: she told a joke and he did not laugh

notes.content: They rest in the shade of a hillside. Ysara watches a hawk circle overhead, higher and higher until it is just a speck against the sky. She wishes she could fly, but not like the hawk — she wishes she could fly like the stars did, if stars can fly.
needle_syns: she wished she could fly like the stars

notes.content: Aldric sits perfectly still while they rest. He does not eat, and he does not look around. He just sits, and Ysara realizes he is not resting; he is waiting. He has been waiting for this day for a very long time.

When they reach the fence post, Thistle the mule will not budge. He has found a patch of sweet clover and he is determined to eat every last leaf. Ysara sings to him, and he ignores her, chewing contentedly.
Ysara asks who named the mule Thistle. Aldric says, 'The last person who owned him.' She asks what the last person was like. Aldric says, 'He was cruel.' She does not ask more.
needle_syns: the last person who owned him

notes.content: At the crossroads, Thistle turns left. Aldric wants to go right. Brugh, who is waiting at the crossroads, says, 'Follow the mule.' They follow the mule. Later, Aldric says he was going the wrong way.

Brugh's stew is made from ingredients Ysara has never seen. It tastes like the earth itself, like walking on soil after rain. She drinks it all and asks for more, and Brugh gives her more, and then he asks his question.

'Which of you is carrying the future?' Brugh asks again. Neither of them answers. The dwarf shrugs and goes back to stirring his stew. 'Neither of you,' he says. 'The mule is.' He pats Thistle on the nose, and Thistle chews.
needle_syns: the mule is carrying the future

notes.content: Mara the ferrywoman is very old. Her skin is like water, rippling when she moves, and her eyes are the color of the river itself. She has been crossing people across the river for so long that she has become part of it.
needle_syns: she has become part of the river

notes.content: The ferry is old wood and it creaks as it moves across the water. Ysara grips the railing and looks down at the river below, and she sees faces in the water, looking up at her. They are the faces of people who crossed before and never made it to the other side.
needle_syns: faces in the water looking up

notes.content: When Aldric pays Mara with his memories, Ysara watches the color drain from his eyes. When he is finished paying, he does not look at her the same way. He looks through her, as if she is not really there. He has paid with too much.
needle_syns: the color drained from his eyes

notes.content: Ysara did not pay with her memories. Mara offered, but Ysara said no. Now she is glad. She remembers everything, and the remembering is heavy, but it is hers. She will not trade it, not for anything.

After the crossing, Aldric does not speak for a long time. When he finally does, he asks Ysara what her name is. She tells him. He nods, but his eyes do not know the name. She is afraid, but she does not say so.
needle_syns: he asked her what her name is
his eyes do not know the name

notes.content: In her dream, the burning cold city is clearer now. She can see the streets, and on the streets there are people running, but they are running in circles. They do not know where to go. The fire does not consume them; it keeps them running forever.

Ysara wakes up shaking. Aldric is awake too, and he is looking at her with an expression she does not recognize. It is not concern; it is recognition. He has seen this before. He has seen her shake like this before, and he does not like it.
needle_syns: he has seen her shake like this

notes.content: The walking becomes easier. Ysara's legs grow strong, and she begins to enjoy it, the rhythm of steps and the changing scenery. She realizes she has been inside her whole life, and the outside world is vast, and she is only just beginning to see it.

At night, Ysara dreams of home, but her home in the dreams is not the frost hall. It is a small house with a garden, and in the garden there are flowers, and a man is weeding, and he looks up and smiles at her, and she knows him but she does not know his name.
needle_syns: dreams of a small house with a garden
she knows him but not his name

notes.content: She tells Aldric about the dream. He listens and says, 'That is not a dream. That is a memory.' He does not explain what he means, and she does not ask. They walk on in silence.
needle_syns: he said it was a memory not a dream

notes.content: The standing stones are taller than she expected. They reach up into the sky like fingers, pointing at something she cannot see. The air around them is cold, colder than it should be this time of year.
needle_syns: the stones reach up into the sky
pointing at something she cannot see

notes.content: One stone is warm. Ysara puts her hand on it and it is warm like a living thing, like an animal sleeping. She does not pull her hand away. She stays there for a long time, her hand on the warm stone, listening to it breathe.

The stone whispers her name again, and this time she hears it clearly. It says, 'Yara.' Not 'Ysara.' Just 'Yara.' She asks Aldric if he heard it. He says no. She wonders if the stone knows her better than she knows herself.

They walk faster now. The road is straighter, and the country is opening up. They are leaving the wild places behind and entering the settled lands, where there are farms and villages and people who live their lives without knowing about wars or pacts.

A child runs past them, chasing a dog. The child does not look at them. The child is busy being a child, and this makes Ysara think about what children are like in the frost hall. There are no children in the frost hall. She does not know why.
needle_syns: there are no children in the frost hall
the child does not look at them

notes.content: Ysara watches the child until the child is out of sight. Aldric notices her watching and says, 'You are looking at her like you are trying to remember something.' She is not sure what she is trying to remember, but he is right.
needle_syns: looking like you are trying to remember

notes.content: Ysara hears a bird sing. She stops walking and listens. She has never heard a bird sing before. The song is so simple and so complete that she stands there for a long time, and Aldric waits for her without saying anything.
needle_syns: the song is so simple and so complete

notes.content: The bird's song stays with her for the rest of the day. It plays in her head like a melody she cannot forget, and she finds herself humming it without meaning to. When Aldric asks what she is humming, she does not know how to answer.
needle_syns: the bird's song stays with her

notes.content: At night, Ysara sees shadows moving at the edge of her sight. They are not animal shadows; they are too tall. She tells Aldric, and he says, 'It's just the wind in the trees.' She is not sure she believes him, but she does not argue.
needle_syns: just the wind in the trees
